mcqs.question: `type User = { name: string }`; `const user = JSON.parse('{"name":42}') as User`; `user.name.toUpperCase()`. This compiles under `strict`. What happens when the last line runs?
options: `TypeError: user.name.toUpperCase is not a function` — the alias and the assertion are erased, so the number reaches the call unvalidated.
The `as User` line throws first, because an assertion checks the value's runtime shape before it narrows.
It returns `42` as a string: `JSON.parse` builds the value from the declared type, so `name` comes back as a `string`.
It fails to compile: `JSON.parse` returns `unknown`, and asserting that to `User` requires a guard first.
mcqs.explanation: Types are erased, so the emitted JavaScript is `JSON.parse('{"name":42}').name.toUpperCase()` and `42` has no `toUpperCase`: the call throws, and nothing at runtime ever read `User`. It compiles at all because `JSON.parse` is declared as returning `any`; `any` overlaps every type, so `as User` is accepted without a diagnostic and the unchecked value flows into a `User`-typed variable. The strongest distractor is the second option, the belief that `as` is a checked cast. It is not — it is a claim made to the compiler and then erased, and the only check that ran was assignability between `any` and `User`, which is always satisfiable. Option three confuses a type with deserialization: no annotation reaches `JSON.parse`, so nothing can turn `42` into `'42'`. The fourth option swaps the lib signature: `JSON.parse` returns `any`, not `unknown`, and that is precisely why the bare `as` is silent — annotating `const raw: unknown = JSON.parse(...)` is the habit that forces a guard.

mcqs.question: `function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] { return obj[key]; }` then `const cfg = { retries: 3, label: 'x' }; const key: string = 'retries'; pluck(cfg, key);` — what does the compiler do with that call?
options: Accepts it and types the result as `unknown`, because `cfg` has no index signature for the checker to look up.
Rejects it: `string` is wider than `'retries' | 'label'`, so no `K` satisfies both the argument's type and the constraint.
Accepts it and types the result as `string | number`, because the constraint widens `T[K]` to every property type.
Rejects it only under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`; with the default flags the call compiles.
mcqs.explanation: `K` is inferred from the argument's declared type, `string`, and then checked against `keyof T`; the diagnostic is literally `Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type '"label" | "retries"'`. Nothing widens to rescue the call either: inference never picks a narrower type than the value it inferred from, so there is no `K` the constraint can accept. The strongest distractor is the third option, because it sounds like how constraints are usually described: a constraint is a filter, not a fallback, and `keyof T` never substitutes for a `K` that failed. The fix is on the caller's side — declare the variable as `keyof typeof cfg`, keep the literal at the call site, or `as const` upstream — and then `T[K]` really does widen, to `string | number`, because `K` is the union and indexed access distributes over it. The first option inverts the mechanism: `K extends keyof T` is exactly what makes `obj[key]` legal inside the body, and an index signature would only move the same hole from `unknown` to `string`. The fourth option attaches a flag that governs index-signature reads; the identical error appears with and without `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (verified on this snippet with TypeScript 5.9.3).

mcqs.question: Under `strict`: `declare const users: User[]; const found = users.find(u => u.id === 2);` — what is `typeof found`, and what happens on `found.name`?
options: `User | undefined`, but only because `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is enabled; under `strict` alone it is `User`.
`User` — `find` is declared on `Array<T>` and returns `T`; only a `readonly` array adds `undefined`.
`User | null` — a missing element is modelled as `null`, and `strictNullChecks` forces you to test for it.
`User | undefined` — the lib signature already says a match may not exist, so `found.name` is an error until you narrow.
mcqs.explanation: `find` is declared in the ES2015 lib as `find<S extends T>(predicate): S | undefined`, so the `undefined` comes from the method's own signature, not from a flag. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` changes index-signature reads such as `users[0]` and leaves `find` exactly as it was. `found.name` is then `'found' is possibly 'undefined'` until `if (found)`, `?.` or an early return narrows it. With `strictNullChecks` off, `undefined` is assignable to every type, so the same `| undefined` stops being visible and `found.name` compiles — the only sense in which the flag 'changes' the type. The strongest distractor is the first option: right type, wrong cause, which is exactly the review comment worth catching, because `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is a separate opt-in outside the `strict` family (https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#strictNullChecks). Option three confuses the two absent values: `find` never produces `null`, and under `strictNullChecks` `User | undefined` is not even assignable to `User | null`. Option two reads `Array<T>` as if every method returned `T`, and `readonly` has nothing to do with it.

mcqs.question: `tsconfig.json` sets `"include": ["src"]` and `"exclude": ["src/legacy"]`. `src/app.ts` imports `./legacy/helper`, and errors from `src/legacy/helper.ts` still appear. Why?
options: `exclude` only stops emission; every `.ts` file under the project directory is still type-checked.
`exclude` patterns must be absolute, so the relative `src/legacy` entry is silently dropped.
`exclude` subtracts from the entry globs only; an import makes the file reachable from an included entry, so it joins the program.
Only an explicit `files` list can keep a file out; `exclude` is ignored whenever `include` is present.
mcqs.explanation: `include`/`exclude` choose the program's roots, and the program is everything reachable from them: the import in `src/app.ts` adds `src/legacy/helper.ts` even though the glob excluded it, which is what the docs mean by `exclude` only changing what `include` finds (https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#exclude). `tsc --listFiles` proves the chain, and a sibling `src/legacy/standalone.ts` that nobody imports stays out — that is the control showing `exclude` did apply. The strongest distractor is the first option, because `exclude` is routinely read as a build tool's ignore list; it filters program construction, not output, so a `noEmit` project still honours it. Option two inverts a real rule: patterns are resolved relative to the directory containing the `tsconfig.json`, which is why `"src/legacy"` matched at all. Option four invents a conflict: `files` and `include` are additive roots, and `exclude` subtracts from `include` regardless of which produced the entry.

mcqs.question: A team replaces `type Status = 'pending' | 'paid' | 'failed'` with a numeric `enum Status`, arguing the enum is safer. Which statement describes what actually changed?
options: The enum is erased at compile time just like the union, so the change is purely syntactic.
Both forms are validated at runtime, but the enum rejects unknown strings earlier.
The enum emits a runtime object — numeric enums also emit reverse mappings — and neither form validates incoming JSON.
The enum's members are exhaustive by construction, while a literal union cannot make a `switch` exhaustive.
mcqs.explanation: A numeric enum compiles to a real object with both name-to-value and value-to-name entries; a string enum compiles to a plain object; a literal union compiles to nothing at all. That runtime artifact is the whole trade-off, and it is also why `Object.keys(Status)` works while a union has no runtime list unless you keep the source array `as const`. The safety claim does not survive a boundary: types are erased, so `JSON.parse` still hands back an unvalidated value that both forms accept until a runtime check rejects it. The strongest distractor is the first one — 'an enum is just a type, so it is erased' — but an enum is one of the few TypeScript constructs that emits JavaScript, which is exactly the cost being weighed. The fourth option inverts the mechanism: a literal union is precisely what makes a `switch` exhaustive, through a `never` default or a `satisfies Record<Status, ...>` map.

mcqs.question: Given `type Label<T> = T extends any[] ? 'array' : 'other'`, what is `Label<string | number[]>` and how would you get one decision for the whole union?
options: `'array'`, because one member of the union is an array; nothing needs to change.
`'other' | 'array'`, because a naked type parameter distributes over the union; wrapping it as `[T] extends [any[]]` gives one decision.
`'other'`, because a union as a whole is not assignable to `any[]`.
`never`, because the conditional cannot choose between two members.
mcqs.explanation: Distribution happens only when the checked type is a naked generic parameter: the conditional runs once per member and the results are unioned, so `string` yields `'other'` and `number[]` yields `'array'`. The strongest distractor is the third option, because its reasoning is correct for the bracketed form — a tuple stops distribution and tests the union as a whole — yet it describes the wrong alias. The `never` option invents an error: conditional types do not fail on unions, they distribute over them. Bracketing is the right move when you genuinely want one decision, for example `type IsArray<T> = [T] extends [any[]] ? true : false`; on a helper that should extract per member, it silently changes the contract.

mcqs.question: Which `on` signature types `value` as `number` in `person.on('ageChanged', value => ...)` and rejects `person.on('agChanged', () => {})`?
options: `on(name: string, callback: (value: unknown) => void): void`
`on(name: `${string}Changed`, callback: (value: number) => void): void`
`on<Key extends string & keyof T>(name: `${Key}Changed`, callback: (value: T[Key]) => void): void`
`on<Key extends keyof T>(name: Key, callback: (value: T[Key]) => void): void`
mcqs.explanation: The template literal builds the permitted spelling from `Key`, and indexed access `T[Key]` supplies the matching property type, so each event name carries its own callback type: `'ageChanged'` is `number`, and a `'nameChanged'` event would take `string`. The strongest distractor is the fourth option, which is structurally close: it constrains `Key` correctly and types the callback from `T[Key]`, but it drops the template literal, so the accepted name is `'age'`, not `'ageChanged'` — the call fails and the derivation is lost. The second option is the other common miss: `${string}Changed` accepts any prefix, so `'agChanged'` compiles and `number` is hardcoded instead of following the property. None of this exists at runtime; the compiler is only checking the literal you pass against the pattern.

mcqs.question: With overloads `parse(value: string): number`, `parse(value: number): string`, and an implementation taking `string | number`, what happens to `const input: string | number = ...; parse(input)`?
options: It is accepted as `number | string`, because the implementation signature takes `string | number`.
It is rejected, because a union argument matches neither overload and the implementation signature is not callable.
It is accepted as `number`, because the first overload is tried first and the union contains a string.
It is accepted, then throws at runtime because overloads validate the argument value.
mcqs.explanation: Overload resolution runs at the call site against the declared signatures, and `string | number` is assignable to neither `string` nor `number`, so no overload applies. The implementation signature exists only to type-check the body; callers cannot reach it. The strongest distractor is the first one, because it treats the implementation as a third overload — a natural read of the source, but not how the API is exposed. The fourth option confuses a compile-time choice with a runtime check: overloads are erased, so nothing inspects the value at runtime. The practical fixes are to add an overload that accepts the union and returns the union, or to drop overloads for a single union parameter with a conditional return type when the overload count starts to grow.

mcqs.question: You add `types/legacy-widget.d.ts` containing `declare module 'legacy-widget' { export function mount(selector: string): void }`, yet `import 'legacy-widget'` still reports a missing declaration file. What is the most likely cause?
options: The file lacks `export {}`, so it is treated as a script instead of a module.
The file is not part of the program — `include`/`files` do not pick it up and nothing imports it — so the compiler never loads it.
`.d.ts` files are only honoured inside `node_modules/@types`.
The `declare module` block must be wrapped in `declare global`.
mcqs.explanation: An ambient module declaration only contributes when the file containing it is part of the program: it has to be matched by `include`, listed in `files`, or reachable through `types`/`typeRoots`. Diagnostics for exactly this case are `tsc --listFiles` and `tsc --explainFiles`, which show whether the file was loaded and by what. The strongest distractor is the first option, because `export {}` does matter here — but in the opposite direction: adding it turns the file into a module, and a `declare module 'legacy-widget'` inside a module is an augmentation of a module that must already resolve, which is precisely what an untyped package does not do. Option three is wrong because local declarations are the documented path for untyped packages, and option four confuses `declare global` (adding globals from inside a module) with declaring a module's exports.

mcqs.question: This compiles. `declare const brand: unique symbol; type UserId = string & { readonly [brand]: 'UserId' }; const id = params.get('id')! as UserId; loadUser(id);` — what safety does the brand actually provide here?
options: None at that boundary: the cast forges a `UserId` from any string; the brand only stops accidental mixing between values that are already branded.
Runtime protection, because the `unique symbol` adds a real property that `loadUser` can inspect.
Full nominal safety, because `as UserId` is rejected unless `brand` is in scope at the call site.
It makes `UserId` and `OrderId` structurally identical, so only naming conventions separate them.
mcqs.explanation: A brand is an extra member added to a structural type, so `string` is no longer assignable to `UserId` while `UserId` is still a `string` everywhere else. That catches `loadUser(orderId)` and stops a raw string from slipping in without a cast — and stops there. The strongest distractor is the second option, because `unique symbol` sounds like runtime machinery; it is not: the marker is type-level only, `typeof id` is still `'string'`, the property does not exist on the value, and `JSON.stringify` round-trips it as a plain string, so no runtime check can see it. Option four is the reverse mistake: the two brands differ by the `'UserId'`/`'OrderId'` literal, which is what makes them incompatible. The honest conclusion is that the cast launders the input, so the guarantee has to come from a validating factory at the boundary.

mcqs.question: A service sets `"experimentalDecorators": true` and decorates methods with `function logged(target: object, key: string, descriptor: PropertyDescriptor) { const original = descriptor.value; descriptor.value = function (this: unknown, ...args: unknown[]) { log(key); return original.apply(this, args); }; }`. A teammate deletes the flag to "move to the standard decorators" and changes nothing else. What happens?
options: It stops compiling, and the contract it was written against is gone: the standard form calls a method decorator with `(value, context)` and expects the replacement to be returned, so there is no descriptor to mutate in place.
Nothing changes: `@logged` is the same decorator under both models, and the flag only selects which syntax the parser accepts.
It compiles and still wraps the method, but loses the type metadata, since standard decorators are annotations that record `context.kind` and cannot replace the decorated function.
It compiles once `emitDecoratorMetadata` is enabled, because the standard form reads the parameter types from that emitted metadata instead of from a descriptor.
mcqs.explanation: The flag is not a syntax switch, it is a semantics switch: `experimentalDecorators` selects the legacy model, and without it TypeScript applies the TC39 standard one, where a method decorator is called as `(value, context)` — the method function plus a context object carrying `kind`, `name`, `static`, `private`, `accessor` and `addInitializer` — and the supported way to change the member is to return a replacement. The legacy body cannot survive that: it declares a third parameter, so the declaration no longer matches the expected decorator type (verified on TypeScript 5.9.3: TS1241, "The runtime will invoke the decorator with 2 arguments, but the decorator expects 3"), and even with the arity silenced the body mutates a descriptor that no longer exists instead of returning a function, which leaves the method unchanged. The strongest distractor is the same-decorator one, because both models are spelled `@logged` at the call site and the flag reads like a parser choice; what it actually selects is how the emitted decorator call is built, which is why a library written for one model does not run under the other. The annotation-only distractor inverts the standard contract: returning a function from a method decorator is precisely how standard decorators wrap behaviour. What the standard model lacks is legacy type reflection (`emitDecoratorMetadata` plus `reflect-metadata`, the crutch behind Angular and Nest DI); if you need to intercept reads and writes, the standard model pairs a field decorator with the `accessor` keyword rather than a `PropertyDescriptor`. The metadata-enabling distractor merges the two pipelines: metadata emission belongs to the legacy world, it changes nothing about the call shape, and no `design:paramtypes` metadata exists under the standard model. Sources: https://github.com/tc39/proposal-decorators and https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-5-0/.

mcqs.question: A button composes two prop sets by intersection: `type BaseProps = { size: 'sm'; onClick(): void }; type BadgeProps = { size: 'lg'; tone: 'danger' }; type ButtonProps = BaseProps & BadgeProps;`. A reviewer says `ButtonProps` is "both shapes merged, with `size` widened to `'sm' | 'lg'`". What does the compiler actually produce, and what does the first use site report?
options: `ButtonProps` is `never`: one key with conflicting types across constituents collapses the whole intersection, so `size`, `onClick` and `tone` all report "does not exist on type 'never'", next to a note naming `size` as the conflicting property.
`ButtonProps` holds every member of both shapes, with `size: 'sm' | 'lg'`, because an intersection collects the options of its constituents.
`ButtonProps` keeps `onClick` and `tone` and turns only `size` into `never`; the contradiction is local to that key, so the rest of the shape survives.
`ButtonProps` keeps `size: 'sm'` and discards `BadgeProps['size']`, because a later constituent overrides a key that an earlier one declared.
mcqs.explanation: `&` requires one value to satisfy both constituents, so the shared key must be assignable to `'sm'` and to `'lg'` at once, which has no inhabitant. TypeScript does not degrade the offending property: it reduces the intersection type itself, and the diagnostic says so — "The intersection 'ButtonProps' was reduced to 'never' because property 'size' has conflicting types in some constituents" — so the first thing that breaks is often an unrelated member: `button.onClick()` reports "Property 'onClick' does not exist on type 'never'" (verified on TypeScript 5.9.3). The strongest distractor is the local-never one, because a local `never` is the recoverable failure people expect and it is how the rule usually gets taught; the reduction happens at the whole-type level, which is exactly why the error surfaces far from the real conflict. The operator-swap distractor swaps `|` and `&`: `|` collects alternatives, `&` demands both, so the value cannot pick one size. The last-wins distractor imports object-spread semantics (`{ ...a, ...b }` lets `b` win) into a type operator that has no ordering at all. The overlap case is the useful nuance, not a fix: when the literals do intersect, the key collapses to the overlap — `('neutral' | 'brand') & ('brand' | 'danger')` is `'brand'` — and the repair is to declare the shared prop once in a common base (`size: 'sm' | 'lg'`) or to strip it from one side before composing, `BaseProps & Omit<BadgeProps, 'size'>`, which is where utility types earn their keep. Source: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html.

scenarios.prompt: Two production reports land on this module and neither is a type error. (1) A payload of `{ "status": "success" }` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toUpperCase')`. (2) A payload of `{ "status": "identical" }` returns `undefined` although the signature promises `string`, so the caller crashes one frame later. Nothing here is red in CI. Explain what the compiler did and did not verify, then redesign the model and the boundary so a malformed payload is rejected with a diagnostic that names the field, and so the handler cannot silently miss a variant.
rubric: Reads the model honestly: `status: string` is not a discriminant, so the `if` narrows nothing and `data!` is the only reason the call compiles.
Traces both symptoms to the boundary: `raw as Result` asserts without checking, and `message!` turns 'maybe absent' into a typed `string` with no runtime evidence.
Rewrites the model as a discriminated union with literal statuses and required per-variant fields, so `{ status: 'success' }` stops being assignable.
Guard takes `unknown`, checks container → discriminant → variant field type, and states the failure contract (throw vs. Result) at the boundary.
Makes the handler exhaustive with a `never` branch and shows that adding a variant breaks the build instead of falling through.

scenarios.prompt: `my-lib` builds cleanly, its own suite is green, and `tsc` writes `dist/`. Then two consumer reports arrive: Node apps fail with `Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find package '@core/parse' imported from .../node_modules/my-lib/dist/index.js`, and TypeScript consumers get `Cannot find module '@core/parse'` pointing into `dist/index.d.ts`. Explain why none of the package's own checks could catch this, then make the published surface resolvable without asking consumers to copy an alias config.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
**Diagnosis.** `paths` is a compile-time mapping and it does not affect emit: `tsc` uses it to find `src/core/parse.ts`, then copies the specifier into the output verbatim, so both `dist/index.js` and `dist/index.d.ts` still say `@core/parse`. The docs put it plainly — '`paths` does not change the import path in the code emitted by TypeScript' — and the publishable-library guidance is to leave it out for exactly this reason (https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/modules/reference.html#paths-does-not-affect-emit). Reproduced on the config above with TypeScript 5.9.3: nothing in `compilerOptions` turns an alias into a relative path.

**Why the package looks healthy.** Every check ran from the repo root, where that same `tsconfig.json` is in effect: `tsc --noEmit` resolves the alias, and the test runner or bundler resolves it with its own mapping. The npm consumer is the first party that never sees that config. Node resolves `@core/parse` with its own algorithm plus the library's `exports`, finds no package named `@core`, and fails; the consumer's `moduleResolution` (`bundler` or `nodenext`) opens `dist/index.d.ts`, meets the same specifier, and reports `TS2307`. Neither failure is a build failure, which is why CI stays green.

**One specifier, two broken contracts.** Runtime resolution and type resolution agree here only by accident, and they break in different places. Fixing just the JavaScript leaves consumers with unresolvable declarations; fixing just the declarations leaves the crash. Treat emitted `.js` and `.d.ts` as one surface.

**Fix A — make the specifier real (smallest change).** An alias inside a single package root buys little; use a relative import and let the entry point be the only public door:

```ts
// src/index.ts
export { parse } from './core/parse';
```

**Fix B — keep the ergonomics with a mechanism the runtime also understands.** Node's `imports` map is the documented replacement for convenience `paths` aliases, and it works for the consumer because it is resolved against the *library's* `package.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "my-lib",
  "type": "module",
  "imports": { "#core/*": "./dist/core/*" },
  "exports": {
    ".": { "types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "default": "./dist/index.js" }
  },
  "files": ["dist"]
}
```

Source imports then read `#core/parse`, `tsc` resolves the key under `node16`/`nodenext`/`bundler`, and the consumer's Node resolves the same key with no consumer-side configuration. Two caveats worth saying out loud: the map must point at files that exist when the compiler runs, so pointing at `dist` implies a build order (project references or a second pass) rather than a free lunch; and inside `exports`, conditions are matched in order, so `"types"` goes first or a `default`/`import` branch matches and the declarations are never reached.

**Fix C — rewrite the alias after compilation.** A bundler or a `tsc-alias`-style step can rewrite `@core/*` in the emitted files. This works, but the rewrite becomes part of the published contract, so it has to be verified on the artifact; a step that silently stops running is worse than no step. Note that the 5.7 `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` flag does not help here — it rewrites relative `.ts` extensions to `.js`, not alias specifiers.

**What is not a fix.** Telling consumers to extend your `tsconfig.json`, publishing `src` instead of `dist`, or leaving `paths` in a published package and hoping the consumer's bundler has the same alias.

**Verification.** `npm pack`, install the tarball into a scratch project, then check both halves: run the emitted JavaScript in Node, and type-check a consumer file under the consumer's own `moduleResolution`. Inspect the tarball too — a `dist` that mentions `@core` is the evidence. The repo's own suite cannot catch this class of bug at all, because it never leaves the directory where the mapping applies.
rubric: Names the mechanism exactly: `paths` is compile-time only, and the specifier survives verbatim in both the emitted `.js` and the `.d.ts`.
Explains the asymmetry — in-repo checks resolve through the same tsconfig, so green tests say nothing about a consumer who has no such config.
Treats runtime and declaration resolution as one contract and fixes both, instead of only the JavaScript.
Moves to a resolvable specifier or a real `exports`/`imports` surface, and is honest about the build-order or rewrite step that option implies.
Verifies by packing the tarball and consuming it from a scratch project — type-checked and executed under the consumer's module settings.

scenarios.prompt: Predict the resolved types of `A`, `B`, `C` and `D`. One of them silently becomes `never` and the bug only surfaces downstream. Explain why, refactor `ArrayElement` so both the array case and the union case behave as documented, and say when the bracketed form is the correct choice instead.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Resolved types: `A` is `string`; `B` is `never`; `C` is `User`; `D` is `User | number`. `Head` is also `never` for the same reason as `B`, so the final assignment fails — and the error lands at the use site, not at the helper.

Why `B` is `never`: distribution over a union only happens when the checked type is a **naked** type parameter. `[T] extends [Array<infer Item>]` wraps both sides in tuples, so the checker makes one decision for the whole union: `string | number[]` is not itself an array, the condition is false, and the declared false branch is `never`. That is the second half of the bug — `never` in the false branch hides the miss. A pass-through helper should return `T` there (`T extends Array<infer Item> ? Item : T`) so a non-array input is carried forward unchanged instead of vanishing; `never` belongs only in helpers whose contract is 'this input is invalid'.

Why the others work: `C` and `D` both use naked parameters. `EnvelopeData` distributes over the two envelope variants, so the `{ ok: false }` branch yields `never` and `User | never` collapses to `User`. `AwaitedData` is recursive and unwraps one level per pass: the `Promise` match binds `P` to the union of envelopes, then the recursive call hits `EnvelopeData`, which distributes again into `User | number`. Each `infer` binds exactly one layer of the pattern, which is why unwrapping `Promise<Response[]>` correctly needs two conditionals, not one.

Refactor:

```ts
type ArrayElement<T> = T extends readonly (infer Item)[] ? Item : T;
```

With the naked parameter, `A` stays `string`, `B` becomes `string | number`, and the `ids` line type-checks. `readonly (infer Item)[]` also accepts `readonly` arrays, which `Array<infer Item>` does not.

Keep the bracketed form when one decision for the whole union is the point: `type IsArray<T> = [T] extends [readonly unknown[]] ? true : false` must not answer `true | false` for `string | number[]`. The choice is a contract decision, not a style one. Finally, none of this exists at runtime: the conditional is erased, so a value-level `Array.isArray` guard does not repair a helper that resolved to `never` — the fix has to be in the type.
rubric: Predicts `A` = `string`, `B` = `never`, `C` = `User`, `D` = `User | number`.
Explains that distribution requires a naked type parameter and that the tuple form suppresses it, so `B` tests the union as a whole.
Names `never` in the false branch as the reason the failure is silent, and chooses the fallback deliberately (`T` for pass-through, `never` for a predicate).
Refactors to the distributing form and accounts for `readonly` arrays, e.g. `T extends readonly (infer Item)[] ? Item : T`.
States when bracketing is correct (`IsArray`-style predicates) and notes that conditional types emit no JavaScript, so no runtime guard compensates.

scenarios.prompt: This module tries to make IDs and money units nominal with brands. Find the places where the compile-time guarantee is forged rather than earned, refactor so the only way to obtain a `UserId` or a `Cents` is a validating entry point, and explain what survives at runtime.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
The brand declarations are fine; the boundary is not. `Brand<T, B>` adds an inaccessible member, which is what makes `UserId` and `OrderId` incompatible despite both being strings — `loadUser(orderId)` is a compile error, and that is the entire win. Everything else here defeats it.

Forgery one: `asUserId` is named like a factory but performs no check. `''`, `'order_9'` or any injected value becomes a `UserId`, and every downstream function now trusts it. A brand must be granted after validation, inside the factory, and the cast must be the last statement: check `/^user_/`, throw or return a `Result`, then `return value as UserId`. The cast is unavoidable — `as` cannot be blocked — so the guarantee is architectural: construction lives in one reviewed module and nothing else casts. Keeping the `brand` symbol module-private (export only the aliases and the factories) removes the temptation and the accidental construction; it does not stop a determined `as`, which is why review and lint rules belong to the design.

Forgery two: `19.99 as Cents`. Two problems in one line. It bypasses the factory, and the value does not match the unit the type claims — cents are integers, `19.99` is a decimal amount. Then `price + 0.3` widens to plain `number`, so the brand was doing nothing there and the re-cast hides both the widening and the unit error. Arithmetic does not carry a brand: for branded numbers you need total functions such as `addCents(a: Cents, b: Cents): Cents` and `toCents(value: number): Cents` with an integer and non-negative check, and raw arithmetic stays out of the typed layer.

What survives at runtime: nothing. `typeof id === 'string'` and `typeof price === 'number'`; the marker property does not exist on the value, `Object.keys` shows nothing, and a JSON round-trip returns a plain primitive. So no runtime check can verify a brand, and a brand never validates external input — the validator at the boundary does.

Worth the friction for exactly the cases here: ids that would be costly to swap, money, units. Do not brand every string. If the value is a class, a `private` or `protected` member already gives the same nominal incompatibility without a convention, and enum members are nominal too; brands remain the lightest option for primitives.
rubric: Locates the failure in the unchecked cast inside `asUserId`, not in the brand declaration.
Explains erasure concretely: `typeof` is still `string`/`number`, nothing is stored on the value, and JSON round-trips as a primitive, so the guarantee is compile-time only.
Catches that `price + 0.3` widens to `number` and that re-casting is a second forgery, plus the unit error in `19.99 as Cents`.
Refactors to validating factories (prefix check for ids, integer/non-negative check for cents) with total helpers for arithmetic.
Justifies branding selectively and names the alternative for classes (`private`/`protected` member) or enums.

scenarios.prompt: Three reports from the invoices screen this week, all with a green build and no type error anywhere. (1) Support sends a screenshot of a "Card declined" banner sitting above a perfectly rendered invoice row. (2) Since the API started returning a fourth status, the badge shows the raw lowercase word `partial` and nothing failed to compile. (3) Two rows read `INV-1 undefined EUR` because a column name was mistyped in the formatter. Write the response model from memory — discriminated union, generic key helper, utility-derived input types — then refactor `badge` and `panel` so each symptom becomes impossible or loud, and explain why the compiler now rejects `{ status: 'error', data: [...] }` and why a fourth status cannot ship without a build error. State where `type` versus `interface` applies, and what still has to happen at runtime.
rubric: The model is a discriminated union with a literal `status` and per-variant fields, and the answer shows both rejected literals: `{ status: 'success' }` (missing `data`) and `{ status: 'error', data: [...] }` (excess property on the selected variant).
The generic uses `K extends keyof T` and returns `T[K]`, not `any` or `unknown`, and the answer names the call-site diagnostic for a mistyped key plus the index-signature caveat.

Exhaustiveness is mechanical — `assertNever(value: never)` in the default, or a `Record<Status, X>` / `satisfies` map — and the answer shows the diagnostic that appears when a fourth variant is added.

Input types are derived with utility types (`Pick` / `Omit` / `Partial`) instead of a hand-reshaped declaration, and the answer states they are compile-time only and cannot delete or freeze fields at runtime.
The boundary and the alias choice are addressed: runtime validation plus normalization at the fetch layer, and the union is a `type` because an `interface` cannot be one.
